# 3  
Integrating Deep Learning in Rolling Process Design for Nanocomposites: A Novel Approach to Strength Prediction

**Amit Tiwari¹[\*](#c03.xhtml#cor1), Payal Bansal², Rachid Amrousse³ and SeitkhanAzat⁴**

*¹Department of Mechanical Engineering, Suresh Gyan Vihar University, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India*

*²Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Poornima Institute of Engineering & Technology, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India*

*³Laboratory of Catalysis and Corrosion of Materials, Faculty of Sciences, University of Chouaib Doukkali, El Jadida, Morocco*

*⁴Laboratory of Engineering Profile, Satbayev University, Almaty, Kazakhstan*

### *Abstract*

The rolling process is considered to be an important step in the production of advanced materials such as nanocomposites, which require the use of some desirable mechanical properties such as tensile strength and hardness. Here in this work, we provide a novel method, for the first time, the neural network (NN) model is embedded into a rolling processing design, which cultivates a reliable and high-precision model capable of predicting the strength of nanocomposites. Our research serves to bridge an important gap that exists in the current intellectual property: robust, flexible tools for predicting nanocomposite strength under a variety of rolling parameters. This work provides a model-based solution to predict fully charged points using an artificial NN by taking advantage of the properties stated above, aiming to predict more accurately and less computationally cheaply. The conceptual model based on the proposed NN training to experimental and simulated data governed nonlinear interactions between parameters such as rolling temperature, number of passes, and initial thickness of sample. The findings showed for the first time that it was possible to forecast strength at a level previously considered state-of-the-art, which could lead to an improvement in real-time process optimization and cost savings. The invention of this new way to incorporate NNs into the design of a rolling process therefore represents a significant advancement in making high-quality nanocomposites more efficiently, accurately, and at a larger scale.

***Keywords*:** Artificial neural network, regression analysis, nanocomposite, mean square error, mechanical properties

## 3.1 Introduction

Rolling is one of the most widely used methods in the industry to shape metals and their alloys through systematically controlled deformation leading to mechanical property tailoring. AZ91 is among the magnesium alloys recognized as an excellent material for various reasons including desirable balance between strength-to-weight ratio, good corrosion resistance, and machinability, which render it attractive to industries such as automotive, aerospace, and biomedical \[[1](#c03.xhtml#ref-1), [2](#c03.xhtml#ref-2)\]. On the one hand, it is well known that the rolling process of AZ91 nanocomposite is difficult due to its insufficiency of hot formability and high microstructural sensitivity to working parameters \[[3](#c03.xhtml#ref-3), [4](#c03.xhtml#ref-4)\]. A deep understanding of the influence of rolling parameters, microstructure evolution, and material behavior is necessary to properly control and predict mechanical properties such as ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and hardness (H). Similarly, Tolouie and Jamaati \[[5](#c03.xhtml#ref-5)\] used FEM to simulate the rolling of AZ91 alloy and provided information related to strain and stress distribution. The only downside of such approach is that it comes with a huge computational expense, in terms of both time and resources, limiting its applicability in real-world situations.

There are several types of particles that can be added to make magnesium matrix composites (MMCs) such as carbides (SiC, TiC, B[4]C, ZrC), oxides (Al[2]O[3], TiO[2]), borides (ZrB[2], TiB[2]), nitrides (AlN, BN, ZrN, TiN), and metals (such as Ti, Cu, Mo) \[[6](#c03.xhtml#ref-6)–[8](#c03.xhtml#ref-8)\]. This phenomenon has been noted repeatedly in the as-cast behavior of MMCs. This has not been restricted to MMCs made using just any type of particulate reinforcement method. For example, it has even been seen in composites made with relatively low-volume fractions of carbide particles smaller than those that would typically break up upon contact with any hard surface particles either worn out by wear and tear due to heating during powder injection molding or cut down as soon as (or under circumstances when) they were compacting from tiles less than 1 cm to be sintered into layers separated vertically along thin planes by sheets extend perpendicular across J pear-shaped blocks used to produce these incorrect crystal structures for crystallographic measurements \[[9](#c03.xhtml#ref-9)–[11](#c03.xhtml#ref-11)\]. In both cases, the results had not worked before because nano-reinforced MMCs developed in the past decade demonstrate that although nanoscale additions can significantly enhance the strength of materials, they may also leave the original matrix tough, making the most significant contribution to MMC evolution \[[12](#c03.xhtml#ref-12), [13](#c03.xhtml#ref-13)\].

Temperature is undoubtedly a stand-out parameter in the rolling process. Hot warm rolling makes dynamic recrystallization (DRX), improving ductility, and can severely refine microstructure, despite lowering the strength \[[14](#c03.xhtml#ref-14)\]. With AZ91 nanocomposites, elevated temperatures have been shown to enhance the dispersion of nano reinforcements leading to improved mechanical performance. Bian *et al.* \[[15](#c03.xhtml#ref-15)\] found that rolling AZ91 alloy resulted in significant grain refinement *via* DRX at temperatures above 300°C, but at the same time detrimental to formability of product due to cracking and poor formability behavior, which is attributed to dynamic precipitation when processed under a lower rolling temperature. Similarly, Srinivas *et al.* and Song *et al.* \[[16](#c03.xhtml#ref-16), [17](#c03.xhtml#ref-17)\] stated that using nano-reinforced AZ91 alloys at intermediate rolling temperatures had high strength and ductility by bonding reinforcement to the matrix material without inducing grain growth.

Mamodiya *et al.* \[[18](#c03.xhtml#ref-18)\] revealed that nanocomposites containing AZ91, which rolled at lower strain rates, tended to show intermediate DRX of the magnetic barkhausen noise (MBN) structure and small equivalent diameters (EDs), leading to improved total elongation. On the contrary, Bian *et al.* \[[15](#c03.xhtml#ref-15)\], during rolling, found that fine strain rates inhibit DRX and lead to the coarser grains, along with low ductility and high anisotropy in mechanical properties.

Meanwhile, the rolling speed affects strain rate directly and has a significant impact on both mechanical and microstructural properties of AZ91 nanocomposites. Excessive rolling speeds have potential to cause nonuniform deformation and lead to localization heating, thereby affecting the microstructure homogeneity and mechanical properties negatively. An uneven grain refinement and lower yield strength were shown in case of higher rolling speed, in a study by Zhao *et al.* \[[19](#c03.xhtml#ref-19)\], which studied the effect of rolling speed on AZ91. Zhao *et al.* reported that a moderate rolling speed in their study gave rise to both uniform deformation and effective nanocrystallization in the AZ91 matrix. Another important parameter that has a major effect on the AZ91 nanocomposites is the percentage reduction in thickness during rolling or the reduction ratio, given that higher reduction ratios tend to cause more intense plastic deformation, resulting in the activation of DRX and grain refinement \[[19](#c03.xhtml#ref-19)\]. On the contrary, very difficult reductions in a go are likely to cause cracking and separations especially for fragile nanocomposites. Li *et al.* \[[20](#c03.xhtml#ref-20)\] found that a reduction ratio of 50% during rolling of AZ91 nanocomposites resulted in the best grain refinement and hence improved mechanical properties; however, higher reduction ratios led to microstructural defects.

Even though rolling the AZ91 nanocomposites offers benefits, it still has some challenges. Both this plane crack and the interface delamination occur relatively easily due to the inherent brittleness of magnesium alloys and further, by adding hard nano-reinforcements to it, which makes rolling more likely to be load path independent \[[21](#c03.xhtml#ref-21)\]. Uniform distribution of nano-reinforcements and prevention from clustering are other problems that continue to haunt. In addition, Luo, A. A. *et al.,* \[[22](#c03.xhtml#ref-22)\], demonstrated what had to be done for optimized rolling parameters leading to defects decrease and property improvement in AZ91 nanocomposites. Although the existing research on rolling of AZ91 nanocomposites has provided useful information concerning the influence in each parameter temperature, strain rate, and reinforcement type, comprehensive studies systematically capturing the synergistic influence of these settings on mechanical and microstructural property development are missing. Furthermore, the impact of sophisticated pretreatment methods and multipass rolling routes on AZ91 nanocomposites has not been sufficiently investigated. Bridging these gaps is important to obtain a complete picture of the rolling process and hence empower it for better material performance.

Machine learning has demonstrated promise in recent advances within material science as well. Yang *et al.* \[[23](#c03.xhtml#ref-23)\] used a predictive neural network (NN) model to predict the tensile strength of aluminum alloys with better performance than traditional method. This success provided the impetus for using NN models in other areas, such as magnesium alloys. In the study by Xu *et al.* \[[24](#c03.xhtml#ref-24)\], the capacity of NNs to model the complex material behavior was illustrated, as a backpropagation NN was used to perceive the hardness of AZ31 after extrusion. Despite the aforementioned progress, there is little literature concerning integrating of NN with rolling process design of AZ91 alloy. Munir *et al.* \[[25](#c03.xhtml#ref-25)\] developed a machine learning model to optimize rolling parameters, but their interest was in process efficiency instead of predicting mechanical properties. According to Zhang *et al.,* there is much scope for the adoption of similar techniques in magnesium alloys, whereas Jang *et al.* \[[26](#c03.xhtml#ref-26)\] showed how deep learners outperformed nondeep models when predicting steel properties during rolling, which otherwise has been considered an unsolved problem within the field.

There is an extreme emphasis on lightweight and high-strength materials leading to material innovation as well the production of components with no alternative. The AZ91 alloy is a crucial material used in many fields, and its rolling process was investigated by a new method for better compatibility with the mechanical properties. To improve the anomaly detection performance of rolling, we introduce a novel paradigm by incorporating NNs into the design of this process. NNs are especially well suited due to their capacity for representing nonlinear systems and approximating complex intervariable relationships, making them a good model for strength prediction of AZ91 alloy under rolling load conditions. This study uses machine learning \[[27](#c03.xhtml#ref-27), [28](#c03.xhtml#ref-28)\] to overcome the current issues while putting forward a strong architecture for minimizing cost and process optimization.

In order to tackle these issues, researchers have been increasingly inclined on using computational tools and especially supervised learning models. During the recent years, artificial NNs (ANNs) have been successfully used as predictive tools in the area of material science having an extraordinary ability to capture nonlinear and complex relationship built-in during materials processing. By integrating ANNs in the optimization of rolling parameters, predictive models can be developed to predict mechanical attributes from input conditions as well as optimize these factors efficiently. In this research, the mechanical property of AZ91 nanocomposite is improved by optimizing rolling parameters with an ANN, a specific type of supervised learning algorithm. This study is the first of its kind to concentrate on embedding supervised learning into optimization for rolling parameters in AZ91 material that has a high relevance but less computationally aided research involved with mechanical property optimization. In contrast to some prior works that might have investigated rolling parameters one by one or only a few of them, the current work takes much more dimensions in an optimization way to evaluate all potential importance along with their interpersonal interactions exerting on mechanical strength. Moreover, the adaptation of ANN as a supervised learning model is relatively new to emulate intricate thermomechanical mechanisms in rolling and therefore sets up an exclusive platform for predictive modeling during alloy design.

The supervised learning process is utilized in this research where ANN model was trained using a number of experimental datasets acquired from rolling trials of AZ91 nanocomposite. The input parameters are different control variables of rolling temperature, number of passes, and thickness before rolling of sample, whereas the output data are mechanical strength measurements as UTS and hardness. The ANN is structured with the sequence of these multivariable inputs in order to predict resultant mechanical properties as input–output variables accurately. Fine-tuning of hyperparameters, such as the number and type of ANN hidden layers/ neurons/activation functions, is performed when training an ANN model (to ensure the capturing by this last one, all intricate relationships occurred between input parameters to mechanical outputs). During supervised learning, the model learns from labeled data with a feedback at every step to diminish prediction error. After learning, the model is used for making predictions to provide estimates of different rolling conditions and determine optimum parameters that improve mechanical strength.

ANN-based supervised learning to provide a new paradigm for rolling parameter adaptation in alloy manufacturing not only increases the accuracy of predictions but also limits the number and range of experimental trials, thus making alloy design more sustainable and cost-effective. This study provides a further addition to the materials science field by sharing an accessible methodology that can be scaled up for other magnesium alloys and process routes. This research aims to bridge this gap by proposing a novel supervised learning model based on ANNs to optimize rolling parameters for better mechanical properties in the AZ91 nanocomposite. This study couples real data with computational simulation for higher accuracy and efficiency of mechanical property optimization, paving the way toward additive material selection tools for engineers and researchers in alloy manufacturing field.

## 3.2 Database Collection

A thorough database has been established based on the review of various studies compiling ~150 samples of AZ91 nanocomposite at different rolling parameters \[[11](#c03.xhtml#ref-11)–[24](#c03.xhtml#ref-24)\]. This information gives ideas about how each element plays its role and their participation in the final material behaviors. On the strength of the above observations, 32 elements are chosen as input variables. There are two output variables corresponding to the desired material properties: hardness (H) and tensile strength (MPa).

**Artificial neural networks:** This dataset is used to train ANN models to estimate these features. For every ANN model, a relationship is developed between the selected input variables and the desired output property. Each output property is segregated for ANN model representation as it encourages individual prediction and later validated on optimization. Such models are critical for the insight into the nonlinear interactions among processing parameters and mechanical properties, which, in turn, will provide a basis for optimizing AZ91 nanocomposite to achieve improved performance.

Data on emissions and performance that were gathered over the course of the experiment were included in the model in the capacity of output parameters. The calculations that are performed by the hidden layers on the weighted inputs result in the production of net inputs, which are then used in conjunction with activation functions to generate the real output, as shown in [Figure 3.1](#c03.xhtml#fig3-1).

## 3.4 Results and Discussion

### 3.4.1 Determining Hidden Layers and Training of ANN

The amount of concealed layers has to be kept to a minimum as much as feasible. ANN is initially assumed to have one hidden layer. In cases where the output is not satisfactory, the number of layers will be raised once the ANN has been trained. In addition, the consequence of the network may be produced by several different functions because of their versatility. For this investigation, the Levenberg–Marquardt function was utilized. [Figure 3.3](#c03.xhtml#fig3-3) shows concealing the selected NN block diagram in ANN Simulink. Three neurons were included in the input layer of the network that was implemented into the MATLAB program, and 10 neurons were included in the hidden layer. [Figure 3.4](#c03.xhtml#fig3-4) shows the chosen NN 3-10-2 contains three neurons in the input layer, ten hidden layers with two neurons in it, and two neurons in the output layer. [Table 3.2](#c03.xhtml#tab3-2) displays the optimum input parameters predicted by the ANN for optimizing the hardness and tensile strength values of AZ91 nanocomposite. The table also includes the predicted values of the response variables determined by the ANN.

The network introduced in this study is a multilayer perceptron network with backpropagation error. The Levenberg–Marquardt function was selected as the training function for the network under development because of its rapid convergence capability. The transfer function was determined by trial and error until the mean square error reached the lowest value in both the training and testing sets. Three separate groups were selected at random from the dataset. When it came to testing and validation, although 15% of the data was utilized appropriately, gathering the network’s details used 70% of the data. The number of epochs was determined to be 1000. After three iterations, the network was able to get the best achievable acquisition error. ### 3.4.2 Mean Square Error Plot of Hardness Value and Tensile Strength Value

[Figure 3.5](#c03.xhtml#fig3-5)a shows the MSE function versus epochs (0–8) from a model trained on AZ91 alloy hardness data. The plot of the MSE is set in a log scale as it can range significantly. There are three different curves for the MSE for train, validation, and test set, and then there is the fourth line as a best validation performance at first. The validation set MSE hits its lowest point around epoch 3 with a value of ~1.5958, labeled as “best validation performance.” After epoch 3, the training error continues to decrease dramatically, obtaining very low MSE values by epoch 8. This slope indicates that the model is becoming better at predicting on the training data, which may imply that the model is overfitting. But at some point, the validation and test errors plateau at a higher level with no further improvement in generalization. The widening performance gap between the training curve and both the validation/test curves after epoch 3 is a sign of overfitting as our model continues to get better on our training set, just not on unseen data (validation and test sets). Here, epoch 3 is regarded as the ideal point of stopping because that is when the model yields minimum error on the validation dataset and best generalization.

[Figure 3.5](#c03.xhtml#fig3-5)b represents the MSE while training to predict the tensile strength of AZ91 nanocomposite for 13 epochs. The lowest MSE that gave the best validation performance is around 1.4103 at epoch 12. This is that point on a plot between the very final model learning and where it best generalizes. This implies that model learning is on the right track to minimize loss function, and we are not seeing overfitting until epoch 12 as MSEs for train, validation, and test set are pretty close to each other. The convergence of these error curves indicates consistent model conduct over datasets, with minor separation between training and validation errors indicating a dominant generalization capability. Adding further training beyond epoch 12 exhibits only marginal advantage in training error and no additional decrease at all in validation or test error hallmarks of potential overfitting where more training is to occur. The smooth downward trending curve and the fact that the lowest point of validation error at epoch 12 were also optimal for predicting the tensile strength of AZ91 nanocomposite, indicating that feature learning in this case was done fairly well. At this point, the minimum square error is as low and accurate to model efficiently the major factors of tensile strength in AZ91 nanocomposite.

### 3.4.4 Function Fit Plot of Hardness Value and Tensile Strength Value

In [Figure 3.7](#c03.xhtml#fig3-7)a, a high-accuracy function fit for predicting hardness values is demonstrated in which nearly no errors can be observed on training/ validation/test set of the dataset. Notice in the top plot that the fitted function (black line) matches very well to the actual target values, which are represented by blue, green, and red markers for training, validation, and test data, respectively. From [Figure 3.7](#c03.xhtml#fig3-7), we can see that the model has able to plot out the correct ranges of hardness, and for most input ranges, it is also retrieving the actual output value as target value, that is, from 60 to 80 or from 110 to 140. The near-equivalence of these two metrics demonstrates the model’s accuracy and generalizability across different subsets of data. There are some small differences at around 85 to 90 and again at around 70, but these deviations are restricted in that they appear only as short distances between the estimated values and actual values. Error distribution stays closely maintained around zero, which shows low error in predictions (shown in the lower portion of the plot). The errors are mostly within ±5, indicating that the model has a good capability to estimate hardness values. The overall accuracy of the function fit is very good with only minor errors across the data, confirming some degree of model capability in making hardness predictions over a significant input space.

The reliability and usefulness of predictions are directly linked to model accuracy. In the case of hardness predictions based on a model, high accuracy means that according to various data points, the model is able to predict actual absolute hardness of AZ91 nanocomposite material, and thus, engineers/researchers can rely upon it. So a high accuracy means that our model learns most things in the data very nicely and can predict all things correctly. This is particularly important for applications where subtle variation in properties of materials can have a direct impact on performance, safety, and durability of the product. High precision (i.e., low prediction error) in all the known data increases trust in model outputs for novel instances as well. Reliable models can distinguish small differences in hardness relevant to quality control and optimization functions of manufacturing or materials design. In this context, having high accuracy, the given model helps to predict hardness for all possible compositions or treatments of AZ91 nanocomposite accurately, which can reduce the dependence on extensive physical testing and may lead to faster developments. On the other hand, poor accuracy may cause the actual hardness values: large deviations and not optimal or even unsafe material choice. In intermediate or critical applications, poor hardness predictions may deliver excessively brittle or soft materials for the application leading to structural failure and shortened component lifespans. Hence, accurate prediction of the model will act as a vital role by providing precise values and eliminating errors to achieve an enhanced decision-making process at last.

[Figure 3.7](#c03.xhtml#fig3-7)b shows functional fitting and error analysis of tensile strength predictions with a high fit for the training, validation, and test datasets. The top plot depicts input (red and blue) and predicted output values (green line) for both the fitted function (black line), train (blue), validation (green), and test (red data outputs). The predictions correspond well to the true target values for most of the ranges of input space (especially from 150 to 180 MPa and between 200 and 260 MPa), indicating reasonable accuracy and consistency. We observe small deviations in some regions like about 160 MPa and at around 220 MPa. As mentioned above, these errors are minimal and mostly within ±5 of the target values. This high accuracy is further confirmed by the bottom plot, which depicts the error distribution as the difference between targets and outputs, with errors centered around zero and within a ±10 range in general. Roughly high error points so close to 160 MPa are no more than slightly challenging prediction points, etc., emphasizing the model precision overall. Indeed, high model accuracy in predicting tensile strength values has great influence on results due to its excellent prediction reliability for practical application purpose. In engineering and material science, predicting the tensile strength accurately helps engineers assess whether such materials are suitable for structural applications where durability and safety need to be ensured. The high reliability eliminates the need for extensive physical testing, thereby saving time and cost, while also ensuring that materials such as AZ91 nanocomposite, and will meet nominal strength specifications. Conversely, if the accuracy is low, then there will be greater deviations that may produce poor quality or unsecure material selections that affect the integrity of a structure. As a result, strong model performance is essential to obtain accurate predictions and thus relevant decisions while accelerating the process of material discovery.

## 3.5 Conclusion

The optimization of rolling parameters for AZ91 nanocomposite using ANNs is another leap forward in the development of materials processing and property enhancement. This study thus examines the complexities of modeling such nonlinear interdependencies using ANN, particularly with respect to the rolling process parameters (rolling temperature, number of passes, thickness before rolling of sample) on hardness and tensile strength responses from processing AZ91 nanocomposite. The novelty of this work is that it uses ANN modeling for rolling optimization that is very difficult considering the interactive effects between thermal and mechanical deformations due to coupled nature in magnesium alloys. However, contrary to traditional approaches, ANN successfully covers the complicated parameter-property space and defines the optimal process conditions, which can yield maximum hardness and tensile strength. The importance of this optimization directly impacts industrial applications, where AZ91 nanocomposite is used for lightweight automotive and aerospace components that require mechanical properties to remain safe and operational.

# 4  
Future Directions in Machine Learning–Driven Nanodevice Fabrication

**Wasswa Shafik^(1,2)**

*¹School of Digital Science, Universiti Brunei Darussalam, Gadong, Bandar Seri Begawan, Brunei Darussalam*

*²Dig Connectivity Researh Laboratory (DCRLab), Kampala, Uganda*

### *Abstract*

We now stand on the cusp of a similar scenario in nanodevice fabrication. As we move into the far sub–50-nm scale, traditional fabrication methods start to falter. There is a transition needed to solve this scaling problem, and the proposed solution lies in machine learning. Over the past few years, there have been several successful and significant attempts to train a learning machine to generate patterns for nanodevices. These strategies overcome traditional limitations, such as grid-based design processes or the time-intensive nature of design, by simulating fabrication or material properties. This opens up new design spaces that save significant time and money. Although this prospect itself is an exciting demonstration of the power of machine learning, our goal is twofold. On the one hand, we wish to overview the current landscape of machine learning for nanodevice fabrication, spread over various applications and techniques. On the other, this chapter pushes the conversation beyond the current state of affairs and explores possible future directions for machine learning–based nanodevice fabrication. We have organized this essay where we start with an illustration of machine learning for different stages of the nanofabrication process. In that process, we also summarize the different methods used in several related experimental studies, which helped researchers achieve rapid prototyping of a number of nanofabrication strategies, as well as rapid quantitative discovery of new and accurate metric space estimators. We then summarize the recent related reviews, which include both commercial hardware and experimental studies. Finally, we discuss various open problems, as well as the future directions in this research space within a broader context.

***Keywords*:** Machine learning, nanodevice fabrication, nanotechnology, predictive modeling, AI in manufacturing, materials science, precision engineering, process optimization

## 4.1 Introduction

Fabrication of advanced nanodevices is becoming more challenging, and conventional fabrication techniques are often not adequate to produce the precision required. This is where machine learning (ML) can play an instrumental role. The precise localization of atoms that ML can achieve at a fast speed using significantly fewer computational resources can guide the fabrication processes and optimize them toward the targeted device design. Linking ML models with domain-specific optimization can guide actual nanodevice fabrication and transform computational simulation and material discovery into an experiment-driven field, solving real-world problems \[[1](#c04.xhtml#ref-1)\]. The past few years have witnessed increasing interest in the collaborative study of nanoscience and nanotechnology with ML, inspired by the increasing amount of research in the respective fields. Fields such as atom prediction, nanoscale contact, catalysis, and electronic design are attracting researchers and finding applications in electronics, drug discovery, catalysis, and energy technologies, to name a few. Overall, integrating computational techniques with nanoscience and technology is expected to continue in the foreseeable future \[[2](#c04.xhtml#ref-2)\].

To date, a large number of review articles describe the successful application of ML in fabricating nanoscale devices. An informed observer will notice that current ML methods are instrumental in identifying trends, exploring high-dimensional parameter spaces with large amounts of computational resources, and determining the potential of a material’s properties, to name a few. Although advances have been made using these methods, the focus must shift to providing fully automated solutions that allow ML predictions to guide diverse experimental contexts. Rapid iterations of experiments will foster the development of breakthrough technologies. Further, a survey of the relevant field of ML-driven experiments at the nanoscale is likely to provide a bibliography of cutting-edge research and insights that touch on several emerging technologies, among other expert systems, as illustrated in [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#fig4-1) \[[3](#c04.xhtml#ref-3)\].

![Figure 4.1 Expert systems.](images/fig4-1.jpg)

**Figure 4.1** Expert systems.

## 4.2 Fundamentals of Nanodevice Fabrication

Nanodevice fabrication is the process of creating nanometer-scale electromechanical structures. These devices are rapidly increasing in importance for a considerable number of applications in healthcare, sensing, security, and computation. The predominant methods for creating these devices rely on modifying matter at the atomic level. Traditionally, lithography has been used to define structures. Predominantly, but not exclusively, etching processes have been used to change physical structures to form complex techniques. This “cut and paste” mentality of lithography and etching of individual atoms and molecules, although tried and true, has its limits and presents new challenges as the size of the hardware and devices continue to shrink. In this work, processes for creating 2D and 3D structures will be covered \[[4](#c04.xhtml#ref-4)\]. These methods have been successful in defining structures, and the current state of the art has feature sizes down to 5 nm. However, pushing beyond these sizes is much more difficult. Applying these standard techniques may not always create the desired pattern or structures and often require trial and error by a skilled operator. Many of these processes are empirical, time-consuming, and expensive to engineer for new processes. New systems that take advantage of ML to embody knowledge of atoms, chemistries, biological processes, and particle interactions could enable us to make faster and more accurate predictions from the troves of data we are collecting. In the world of technology, rational design may sound like a distant and less likely possibility, but the introduction of techniques to perform dimensionality reduction to large datasets allows us a better understanding of too large and complex datasets \[[5](#c04.xhtml#ref-5)\].

### 4.2.1 Traditional Methods

Direct writing, photolithography, X-ray lithography, electron beam lithography, and ion beam lithography are direct-write fabrication methods with high resolution. Photolithography is the most widespread optical lithography technique where a desired optical pattern is projected onto a radiation-sensitive material. Chemical vapor deposition is another commonly used fabrication method where a desired material is deposited on a substrate surface. The chemical vapor deposition–generated film has high uniformity and high adhesion between the film and the substrate. The combination of chemical vapor deposition and photolithography shows advancements in transferring pattern density. However, in traditional methods, the time-consuming process, expensive high-quality material required, and scalability limit development in fabricating functional, reliable nanodevices \[[6](#c04.xhtml#ref-6)\].

The traditional methods for nanofabrication can be classified according to the fundamental mechanism into two subcategories: one is a chemical-based method, and the other method is the direct write lithography method. Regardless of the method’s success in advanced manufacturing, there are still many challenges in the current fabrication processes, especially when it comes to emerging nanotechnologies. Material loss during fabrication and the requirement of feedstock repositioning are some significant drawbacks. Swelling of the polymer during lithography limits pattern density and size. Massively parallel writing techniques with large field size areas significantly increase the cost of the system; patterning nanometerscale resolution over centimeter-scale areas is challenging as well. A focused electron beam and ion beam produce charging, resist heating, etc., which readily damage device materials and generate side-effect etching. These situations mentioned above place urgent requirements for innovations and material development of fabricating technologies. Consumer demands for electronic devices have dramatically increased nowadays \[[7](#c04.xhtml#ref-7)\]. Embracing the next step in nanoelectronics and electric devices through the use of ML to aid in nanodevice fabrication design and manipulation is essential and timely.

### 4.2.2 Emergence of ML

The past 5 years have seen an explosion in ML algorithms—transformative advances that are changing virtually every aspect of science, technology, and social systems. These algorithms are capable of analyzing multidimensional, often large datasets, using patterns too complex to be identified using traditional and intuition-based approaches. Nanodevice fabrication consists of a vast number of parameters that can change behavior, including defect density, anisotropies, thermal fluctuations, and structural defects that can synergize across multiple devices and fabrication dimensions. In such a high-dimensional parameter space, predicting nanodevice phenomena—e.g., resistance switching, threshold voltage, and critical current—is complex and necessitates the systematic study of a millimeteraccurate multidimensional fabrication space through thousands of fabrication steps. Traditional approaches to such multidimensional fabrication spaces, large datasets, and complex device–fabrication relationships involve fabrication space division to look for simple 1:1 correlations. ML can consider all device–fabrication interactions at once \[[3](#c04.xhtml#ref-3)\]. ML can carry information through the fabrication process optimally and efficiently. Furthermore, it can recognize nontrivial patterns in the multidimensional spaces that manifest during fabrication.

Through deep learning methods, ML is capable of sifting through a combinatorially large number of nanodevices to look for multipoint correlations involving complex device fabrication, constituent, and environmental interactions. ML also holds its place with rapid and real-time statistical analysis for intentionally destructively probed, large nanodevice statistical ensembles. This provides accelerated device learning on targeted, critical failure, and multiterminal science experiments and a Bayesian approach to sensor data collection, critical for ubiquitous constrained, mobile, and tightly packed dimensional analysis currently taking place in associated nanoelectronic fabrication processes. The comprehensive review of past algorithms’ demonstration capabilities of ML algorithms in nanoengineering ranges from discovering device behavior to execution path optimization and improvement of off-normal fabrication process capabilities. New algorithms are rapidly demonstrating their capabilities to predict nanoevents and determine optimal process sequence paths and termination conditions. This ML revolution in nanoevents is incremental, with many intermediate successes and rigorous comparison study results from scientific communities \[[8](#c04.xhtml#ref-8)\]. Close interactions between fabrication process controls further highlight off-normal fabrication that ML, anneal optimization, and device physics enable new research and innovation only in tight collaboration with their respective interdisciplinary communities. [Table 4.1](#c04.xhtml#tab4-1) illustrates critical analysis by directly comparing algorithms in the context of real nanofabrication challenges, helping identify where certain ML methods excel and where they may fall short.

## 4.3 ML Techniques in Nanodevice Fabrication

Scientists have adopted a host of ML techniques to empower the nanodevice fabrication process. These include not only the time-tested supervised learning methods but also unsupervised and reinforcement learning (RL). The three learning paradigms play unique roles in their own right, but what unifies the ML linkage to nanodevice fabrication is the effort to improve fabrication through greater process control and material accuracy when fabrication accuracy is the ultimate measure of the effectiveness of fabrication processes. The different ML techniques, in this sense, contribute complementary roles to future advances in fabrication processes. Supervised learning models represent a common approach for predictive modeling tasks, particularly when labeled training data are available. On its part, unsupervised learning methods provide a complementary approach for recognizing and exploiting data patterns that exist in fabrication data \[[4](#c04.xhtml#ref-4)\]. These are especially useful where the data do not come prelabeled with measured outputs, such as we do have in supervised learning methods in electronic measurement systems. Unsupervised techniques also include dimension reduction and subsequent visualization. RL has increased interest in the fabrication space as a tuning mechanism that can be especially useful in large and complex systems that require action sampling to determine the best conditions. RL can be involved in the process of making an optimizing decision in a complex space involving multiple competing objectives. The choice of learning technique is often led by the existence or nonexistence of labeled datasets and the fidelity of simulation models for a given process \[[12](#c04.xhtml#ref-12)\]. More recently, approaches that combine learning paradigms have been developed with applications in the optimization of complex multivariate processes. From early on, the importance of the combination of methods to investigate complex processes and models has been explored. We can therefore expect the maturation of the different learning techniques, and their associated computation will guide the development of the field in the coming years \[[5](#c04.xhtml#ref-5)\].

### 4.3.1 Supervised Learning

Supervised learning requires a “teacher” who provides the learning process with a labeled dataset (i.e., data accompanied by the target output). It then learns correlations between this training dataset and the corresponding labels, instance by instance, and uses these correlations to create a model that can predict the desired output given new, unseen data. Consequently, the quality of the learning process and the predictive performance of the model are determined by the quality and representativeness of the labeled training dataset. An advantage of supervised learning over unsupervised learning is that the training signals can provide an immediate way to update the model’s weights during training. This feedback can be used by optimization algorithms to directly influence the evolution of the distribution of the weights throughout the convergence process \[[10](#c04.xhtml#ref-10)\]. Whenever a designer is interested in optimizing some aspect of a nanodevice, the most straightforward approach is to follow a supervised learning strategy. This means that some labeled simulation data are used to build an ML model. Once the model is satisfactorily trained, it predicts the performance factor from the choice of design parameters. This design choice can therefore be selected to optimize the device’s performance.

In this regard, two main categories of supervised learning techniques are desirable: those that are capable of learning continuous function approximations, catalogs, and relationships (regression models) and those that excel at stratifying a space and finding natural classes (classification algorithms). Supervised learning is a natural approach for designing efficient fabrication processes, a perfect example of which can be found in supervised fast epitome mapping techniques. A large amount of quantitative structural information on epitaxial thin films is required to calibrate an evolution model efficiently. In addition to having up to nine independent structural parameters, many of these structures require a nonstandard configuration file due to in-plane frozen dimensions. Producing such simulation data is too expensive for traditional adaptive strategies, but if even a tiny portion of these data is already available, it is suitable for training \[[9](#c04.xhtml#ref-9)\]. It is also strictly controlled and should be highly predictive; mistakes in the training data may result in unsuitable experimental directions. ML has several applications, as sampled in [Figure 4.2](#c04.xhtml#fig4-2).

### 4.3.2 Unsupervised Learning

More subtleties between informatics approaches and materials applications exist. For instance, unsupervised learning techniques complement supervised methods. This future technology projection paper aims to show that ML techniques in unsupervised learning can dramatically impact the way materials are designed. In this section, we will discuss unsupervised learning in a factory. Unlike supervised learning, which requires labeled data, unsupervised learning can discover hidden patterns in data without labels. There are several formulas for unsupervised learning. For example, clustering separates data into different modules based on an intrinsic characteristic within the variables. Applications in fabrication occur when some internal relation between processes and intrinsic values, such as the setup design, can classify some parts as delaminated or incorrect. In this way, factories can avoid building fabricated parts that are not within specifications. Trade-offs often exist between fabrication designs, and insights into the relationships between the fabrication design parameters are essential \[[3](#c04.xhtml#ref-3), [6](#c04.xhtml#ref-6)\]. Polycrystalline samples are full of system noise and can be challenging to characterize using human inspection, and in such situations, unsupervised methods can be applied to datasets with even low signal-to-noise ratio. Thus, invaluable insight exists in scenarios in which robust labeling is unavailable.

![Figure 4.2 Application of machine learning.](images/fig4-2.jpg)

**Figure 4.2** Application of machine learning.

Another approach in unsupervised learning is dimensionality reduction. A new representation of the data is made such that ways to differentiate are optimized. Insights can be extracted so trade-offs in the M and N can be applied to create maximum differentiation in multimedia. The total welding energy of a nanoworld can be extracted using the basis. These techniques can not only identify insufficient or incorrect parts but also identify out-of-model behavior that is undesirable. The representation can be used in downstream supervised learning, testing, and models to show accurate relations of data. Rather than focusing on throughput, this ML approach has more emphasis on process evaluation and optimization, including using these representations in the context of regulatory aspects. Focus sensing for process development and control would be of interest and represents a potential integration point for the suggested movement toward image-based processing \[[5](#c04.xhtml#ref-5), [11](#c04.xhtml#ref-11)\]. These future directions should be explored in experimental research, with the intent of developing a manufactured product.

### 4.3.3 Reinforcement Learning

RL is fundamentally derived from behaviorist psychological theories and focuses on ensuring that an agent acts in a particular desired manner. The main difference with other ML techniques is that RL does not look for or require a correct action or decision for each state. Instead, the aim is for the policy to take the system from an initial situation into a final decision or state to have a cumulative high reward. The RL policy is shaped over time through a series of trial-and-error interactions with the environment. Instead of focusing on real-time optimization of each action sequence like in supervised learning, RL maximizes long-term rewards and is well-suited to applications where the goal is to learn a policy for sequential decision-making \[[6](#c04.xhtml#ref-6)\]. To perform their tasks, a variety of RL strategies have been adopted, such as Q-learning, trial and error learning, dynamic programming, and state–action–reward–state–action (SARSA).

Implementations of RL for optimization typically lie in Q-learning and deep Q-networks and have been adopted to optimize computationally expensive processes that require long-term consideration and cannot be achieved using any other method in a real-time setting. Furthermore, RL models also highlight a more adaptive capability where, rather than inferring a policy that optimizes local variables, they are able to make adaptive decisions to maximize efficiency and even overcome disturbances in the process or previous risks that may have been taken \[[4](#c04.xhtml#ref-4)\]. Examples of studies looking into applications of deep Q-learning in fabrication environments highlight that these strategies are capable of learning from continuous feedback about the environment and selecting the best possible action at each time step to guide the process toward a target, and initial results from their applications have been promising. RL is therefore one of the main techniques proposed to deal with these challenges and is actively being analyzed as one of the future areas of investigation for the field of adaptive fabrication, evaluation of process parameters, and their optimization through ML, as presented in [Table 4.2](#c04.xhtml#tab4-2). Current discussions around this application even go as far as to say that the implementation of RL in adaptive fabrication processes would represent a transformational system in comparison with developments in dynamic structure fabrication \[[1](#c04.xhtml#ref-1)\].
